documents.abstract: Background Digital health interventions have considerable potential to improve healthcare access, quality, and efficiency. Despite increasing adoption, many interventions fail to achieve sustainable implementation or progress beyond pilot phases because they are insufficiently integrated with user needs, organizational workflows, and health system contexts. Although human-centered design (HCD) has improved the usability and acceptability of digital health technologies, its application frequently remains confined to early design activities and is rarely integrated with implementation science throughout the implementation lifecycle. Objective This study aimed to develop a multi-level, human-centered design framework informed by a cross-project methodological synthesis integrating participatory design and implementation science to support the design, implementation, evaluation, and scale-up of digital health interventions. Methods A cross-project methodological synthesis was conducted using complementary digital health implementation studies undertaken in Kenya. The empirical corpus included studies spanning adolescent mental health, neonatal clinical decision support, digital health infrastructure, generative artificial intelligence, and frugal digital health innovation. Framework development followed an iterative analytical process combining thematic synthesis, constant comparative analysis, and abductive reasoning. The synthesis organized recurring methodological themes into an integrated framework spanning user, workflow, and system perspectives across the digital health implementation lifecycle. Results The synthesis identified recurring methodological processes that consistently contributed to successful digital health implementation, including contextual understanding, participatory stakeholder engagement, iterative refinement, workflow integration, organizational readiness, governance, and sustainability. These findings informed the development of a multi-level framework structured around six iterative implementation phases: Understand, Co-design, Prototype, Evaluate, Implement, and Scale, and three interconnected analytical levels: user (micro), workflow (meso), and system (macro). The framework conceptualizes digital health implementation as a continuous sociotechnical process in which sustained adoption and scale-up depend upon coordinated alignment among these three levels throughout the implementation lifecycle. Conclusions This study advances human-centered design by integrating it with implementation science through an empirically derived, lifecycle-oriented methodological framework for digital health implementation. The proposed framework may provide researchers, developers, practitioners, and policymakers with a structured approach for designing, implementing, evaluating, and scaling digital health interventions while supporting sustainable, context-responsive, and equitable digital health transformation.

This study examines the effectiveness of Task-Based Language Teaching (TBLT) in fostering critical thinking skills among intermediate-level English as a Foreign Language (EFL) learners. A quasi-experimental design was employed with 64 intermediate EFL students randomly assigned to an experimental group (n = 32) that received TBLT instruction and a control group (n = 32) that followed a conventional presentation-practice-production approach over a 12-week period. Critical thinking was measured using a modified California Critical Thinking Skills Test adapted for language learners and a task-based performance rubric assessing analysis, evaluation, inference, and argumentation. Results indicated statistically significant gains in the experimental group across all critical thinking dimensions (p < .01), with particularly strong improvements in analysis and evaluation. Qualitative data from learner reflective journals and classroom observations further revealed that authentic, meaning-focused tasks encouraged deeper cognitive engagement, perspective-taking, and reasoned decision-making. The findings suggest that carefully designed TBLT sequences can simultaneously advance linguistic competence and higher-order thinking skills. Implications for EFL curriculum design and teacher training are discussed.

Background University teachers’ occupational wellbeing and emotional exhaustion are relevant occupational-health concerns in higher education. As generative artificial intelligence becomes embedded in teaching work, AI acceptance may represent a perceived, context-specific appraisal of whether AI is usable for intercultural teaching tasks. This study developed a preliminary measure of AI acceptance for intercultural teaching and examined its cross-sectional associations with teacher resources and occupational-health indicators. Methods This two-sample cross-sectional study used Sample A to examine the empirical behavior of the AI Acceptance for Intercultural Teaching Scale and Sample B to test measurement validity and occupational health associations. IBM SPSS Statistics 27.0.1 was used for descriptive statistics, EFA, Cronbach’s alpha, correlations, and regression analyses. CFA and SEM were conducted in R 4.6.1 (lavaan 0.6.21, lavaan.mi 0.1.0, and mice 3.19.0) using robust maximum likelihood (MLR) estimation; CR and AVE were calculated from standardized CFA loadings, and HTMT from item correlations. Hypothesis tests used non-imputed scale-score regressions; multiple imputation (mice, m = 5) with D2-pooled CFA/SEM model tests served as sensitivity analysis, and indirect-association bootstrap intervals were sensitivity summaries rather than formal D2-pooled tests. Results The AITA items were suitable for factor analysis in Sample A (KMO = 0.940), but the exploratory loading pattern did not cleanly reproduce the theorized four TAM-based dimensions. In Sample B, the overall AITA score showed good internal consistency (alpha = 0.858), whereas the four subdimensions showed substantial overlap and weaker reliability and convergent-validity evidence. AI acceptance was positively associated with intercultural teaching self-efficacy and autonomous teaching motivation. Self-efficacy was associated with both occupational wellbeing and lower emotional exhaustion, whereas autonomous motivation was associated primarily with occupational wellbeing. Direct associations between AI acceptance and the occupational-health outcomes were not significant. Conclusion The present findings provide preliminary evidence for using the overall AITA score as a context-specific measure of AI acceptance in intercultural teaching. The results also show cross-sectional associations between AI acceptance and teacher-resource variables, but they do not establish causal effects, mediation, or intervention effectiveness. The four TAM-based dimensions should be treated as provisional content facets requiring further validation.

The ways in which developmental psychology have been taught in university undergraduate and graduate environments differ when delivered in in-person or online settings. This commentary reviews the enablers and barriers of online and in-person pedagogical teaching of developmental psychology, particularly in the post-COVID era of generative AI. Enablers to online teaching primarily centre on the flexibility in how and where students learn, while barriers relate to the number of completed assessments and the amount of content students are required to retain across shortened teaching terms. Enablers to in-person teaching comprise face-to-face tutorials and the opportunity for assessment scaffolding, while barriers include the continuity and ongoing nature of student assessment. In addition, this commentary specifically draws on the teaching and research experiences of the author in identifying a four-pronged approach to improving the delivery of developmental psychology in both in-person and online teaching environments: 1) Constructivism (active engagement), 2) Retrieval practice (memory consolidation), 3) Metacognitive scaffolding, and 4) Motivational design (Self-Determination Theory). It then presents a series of recommendations to this effect, ranging from weekly student reminders and embedding consistent self-test materials throughout the course, to leveraging generative AI in curriculum design and assessment and integrating optional dates or flexibility for student submissions. Finally, it concludes by offering insights about the future of generative AI, including its use and application in developmental psychology, regardless of how the discipline is delivered and taught in the future.

Digital ethics has become a central concern in education as artificial intelligence (AI), generative AI, learning analytics, and data-driven systems are increasingly embedded in teaching, learning, research, and institutional decision-making. Despite rapid growth in scholarship, the literature remains conceptually dispersed, making it difficult to identify dominant ethical concerns, educational responses, and unresolved research gaps. This systematic literature review synthesizes recent scholarship on digital ethics in education by examining ethical implications of AI and generative AI, ethics education and professional development, and ethical dilemmas within professional and institutional practice. The review followed the PRISMA 2020 framework. Searches were conducted in Scopus and ERIC and were limited to English-language peer-reviewed journal articles published in 2024 and 2025. The searches identified 560 records (408 from Scopus and 152 from ERIC); following screening, eligibility assessment, and quality appraisal, 20 studies were retained for qualitative synthesis. The findings converge around three interrelated themes: ethical implications of AI and generative AI; ethics education, ethical training and professional development; and ethical challenges within professional, institutional and data-intensive practice. Overall, the review shows a shift from abstract ethical principles toward applied, context-sensitive ethical competence and governance, while empirical validation and policy evaluation remain limited. The review supports the development and testing of integrated ethical frameworks to guide responsible digital transformation in education.

documents.abstract: The advancement of Artificial Intelligence (AI) in the educational field has expanded teaching and learning possibilities, but has also sparked important ethical and philosophical reflections. This study aimed to map and analyze the scientific literature on the ethical dimensions of AI in teaching and learning processes through a systematic literature search. The search was conducted in the Web of Science database, using the descriptors "Artificial Intelligence" AND "ethics" AND "education." Initially, 1,822 articles were identified; after applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 155 documents remained, of which only 9 comprised the final review. The analysis revealed three main themes: ethical dilemmas related to privacy, algorithmic biases, and student autonomy; philosophical discussions about the role of AI in the teacher-student relationship; and teachers' responsibility when mediated by intelligent technologies. It is concluded that, despite the potential of AI to transform pedagogical practices, theoretical and normative gaps still persist that demand greater scientific and political depth, especially in the development of solid ethical frameworks that guide its application in the educational context.

Introduction The “Destiny Machine” metaphor reveals an ethical concern: big data and artificial intelligence, operating as a data-power social machine, manipulate individuals with pre-determinacy as the core logic. At cognitive-information and behavioral decision-option levels, this manipulation appears as cognitive manipulation by recommendation algorithms and decision-making manipulation by automated decision systems. To uncover its psychological mechanisms and ethical risks, this paper builds a framework integrating ethics and psychology. Methods The Destiny Machine is transformed into an analytical tool with three dimensions: pre-determinacy, irresistibility, and concealment. Drawing on dual-process theory, automation bias, moral disengagement, and psychological reactance, it analyzes how non-invasive intelligent technologies psychologically manipulate individuals and shape their ethical risks, adopting the human-centered approach as the guiding principle for governance. Results Cognitive manipulation by recommender systems, typified by TikTok, leaves users unaware that their cognitive preferences are being systematically reshaped, keeping them imperceptibly immersed. Algorithms achieve this by activating Type 1 processing while bypassing Type 2 scrutiny, confining information to relevance channels, and exploiting automation bias and complacency to lower cognitive vigilance and suppress psychological reactance. Indulging in information cocoons widens users’ cognitive distance from the lifeworld, dissolving their moral attributes as ethical beings. Decision-making manipulation by automated decision systems is most evident in autonomous vehicles’ trolley-problem dilemmas, where passengers’ lives are reduced to quantifiable weights. The system pre-sets decision rules and allows remote intervention at the design end; opaque decision-making subjects and logic, millisecond-level deadlines, and impossibility of exit jointly pre-lock passengers’ fate before the accident occurs. It likewise exploits cognitive processing traits and automation bias, while dispersed agency makes responsibility attribution—and thus psychological reactance—difficult. Pre-coding an individual’s fate at the behavioral decision-option level may deconstruct their meaning world. Discussion Under the Destiny Machine metaphor, such manipulation erodes not only individuals’ autonomy but also their responsibility as moral subjects. Guided by the human-centered approach, it proposes governance schemes with clear actors, sound measures, and reliable benchmarks: a cognitive immune system of transparency and empowerment for cognitive manipulation, and a human-machine collaborative scheme of accountability and remedy for decision-making manipulation, rebuilding passengers’ trust to help them escape.

documents.abstract: The fast growth of artificial intelligence (AI) has created strong interest in how it can change higher education. AI tools brought new useful ways into undergraduate teaching, with the main goal of understanding how AI is currently being used in educational settings. Based on a review of recent studies and learning theories, this paper examines how tools such as intelligent tutoring systems, generative AI platforms, flexible learning technologies, and AI-supported feedback are changing teaching methods at the undergraduate level. The findings show that AI, when used carefully and fairly, can make learning more personal, increase student interest, and help teachers make better decisions based on student data. However, important challenges remain, such as concerns about fairness, student access to technology, teacher readiness, and the risk that students may stop thinking deeply on their own. The paper ends by suggesting a practical guide for using AI in teaching in a responsible and educationally sound way, and it calls for cooperation among schools, teachers, and government leaders to make the most of AI in undergraduate education.

Abstract Background In Indonesia, community health workers (CHWs) play a key role in collecting routine health data through digital platforms. In Malang City, the electronic Elderly Management Information System (e-EMIS) is used to record health screening data for older adults. However, CHW engagement in routine data entry is essential for ensuring that completeness, timeliness, and coverage of these data are optimal in primary care settings. Aim To examine the level of CHW engagement in using e-EMIS and to identify perceived barriers associated with low engagement among CHWs in Malang City, Indonesia. Methods A cross-sectional survey was conducted among CHWs working at integrated health service posts. Of the 645 CHWs nominated by community health centres, 615 CHWs completed a semi-structured self-administered survey. Data were collected on socio-demographic characteristics, mobile-phone ownership and usage, experiences with e-EMIS, exposure to training, and perceived barriers to system use. Descriptive statistics were used to characterise e-EMIS engagement patterns, while Chi-square tests were applied to examine associations between socio-demographic variables, support systems, digital access, and training experiences with e-EMIS use. Results Nearly all CHWs (99.7%) owned a smartphone, and 71% reported intensive use, indicating moderate-to-high levels of digital access. Despite this, only 39% of CHWs had ever used e-EMIS. The majority of CHWs (77.6%) had never received e-EMIS-related training, and among those trained (n = 129), 73% reported that training had occurred more than one year earlier. Intrinsic motivation to use e-EMIS was high (98.5%). Older age and training exposure were positively correlated with e-EMIS engagement. The most cited barriers included lack of community and institutional support, limited training opportunities, and the absence of financial incentives. Conclusion Despite near-universal smartphone ownership and moderate-to-high levels of digital access among CHWs, sustained use of e-EMIS remained sub-optimal. This gap in system uptake underscores the need for stronger engagement strategies to support CHWs in digital reporting. Targeted investment in regular training, user-friendly digital system design, supportive supervision, and enabling health policies is critical to improving CHWs engagement with e-EMIS and strengthening the reliability of community-level health data.

This research paper examines the protection of ethical voice in workplaces where artificial intelligence (AI) supports or influences decisions affecting employees. It focuses on a critical human-centred question: when AI participates in recruitment, performance evaluation, task allocation, customer service, or managerial decision-making, do employees have the right and the psychological safety to understand, question, challenge, and seek correction of AI-supported decisions? The paper analyses the relationship between psychological safety, AI transparency, meaningful human oversight, and employees’ willingness to raise concerns or challenge potentially unfair or harmful automated decisions. It draws on academic literature, international governance frameworks, regulatory guidance, and documented real-world cases, including AI bias in recruitment, algorithmic grading, automated welfare fraud detection, and workplace monitoring. The study identifies major governance risks, including lack of transparency, automation bias, weak accountability, absence of safe grievance mechanisms, and insufficient human review. It proposes the Ethical Voice Model for AI Governance, based on four pillars: transparency, fairness, human oversight, and accountability and appeal. The paper concludes that protecting ethical voice is essential for responsible AI governance, workplace fairness, human dignity, and sustainable institutional trust. It provides practical recommendations for organisations, policymakers, compliance professionals, and AI governance practitioners.

documents.abstract: This study examined the influence of Artificial Intelligence (AI)-driven research methodologies on lecturers' productivity in Lagos State University (LASU), Ojo Campus. The growing integration of AI tools such as Machine Learning (ML), Natural Language Processing (NLP), and ChatGPT into academic research and teaching, alongside concerns about lecturers' research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness in Nigerian universities, motivated the study. Specifically, the study sought to ascertain lecturers' awareness of AI-driven research methodologies, examine their knowledge of ML, NLP and ChatGPT, determine their perception of these tools in enhancing research quality and academic productivity, and establish the influence of the tools on research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness. A descriptive survey research design was adopted, with a sample of 165 lecturers drawn from seven faculties and two schools across Lagos State Owned Universities. Data were collected using a researcher-designed instrument, the Artificial Intelligence Driven Research Methodologies and Lecturers' Productivity Questionnaire (AIDRMLPQ). Out of 189 copies of the questionnaire distributed, 165 were properly completed and returned, giving a response rate of 89.2%. Data were analysed using descriptive statistics (mean and standard deviation) and Pearson Product Moment Correlation at the 0.05 level of significance. Findings revealed a significant positive relationship between the adoption of AI-driven research methodologies and lecturers' research efficiency (r = 0.742), between knowledge of ML, NLP and ChatGPT and academic productivity (r = 0.781), between lecturers' perception of AI tools and research quality (r = 0.766), and between AI tools utilisation and research efficiency, publication output, and teaching effectiveness (r = 0.754). The study concluded that AI-driven research methodologies play a significant and positive role in enhancing lecturers' productivity at LASU, and that institutional support and structured training remain critical to maximising the benefits of AI in higher education. It was recommended, among others, that the University organise regular training on AI tools, develop clear policies on ethical AI use, and invest in AI-compatible infrastructure to support lecturers' effective adoption of AI in research and teaching.

documents.abstract: This study analyzed the paradigmatic evolution of human factors in aviation and operational safety, aiming to understand conceptual transformations related to human performance in complex sociotechnical systems. This is a qualitative, historical-epistemological, and analytical-reflective integrative review grounded in Whittemore and Knafl, Torraco, Braun and Clarke, and Levac, Colquhoun and O’Brien. Searches were conducted in Scopus, Web of Science, PsycINFO, PubMed/MEDLINE, ScienceDirect, and SciELO, as well as institutional aviation safety documents. The final corpus comprised 81 studies. Findings revealed a progressive shift from models centered on individual human error toward cognitive, organizational, systemic, and adaptive approaches. Nevertheless, limitations remain regarding fragmentation between cognition, physiology, emotion, and human-automation interaction. It is concluded that contemporary human factors require integrative models capable of understanding human performance as a dynamic and multimodal phenomenon in complex operational environments.

Introduction As noted in successive OECD assessment reports, global education systems are shifting from standardized assessments toward prioritizing students’ psychological wellbeing and autonomous agency. However, cross-cultural quantitative evidence regarding how these macro-policy transformations relate to students’ micro-psychological perceptions and academic behaviors remains limited. Methods Utilizing a cross-sectional survey, this study analyzed data from 1,309 university students in Shanghai, China, and Kazakhstan. Multi-Group Confirmatory Factor Analysis and Structural Equation Modeling (SEM) were employed to examine the structural associations and measurement invariance among Perceived Educational Transformation (PET), Intrinsic Motivation (IM), and Learning Engagement (LE). Results The three-factor model demonstrated strict measurement invariance across both samples. SEM findings indicated that IM partially mediated a significant indirect associative mechanism the positive structural relationship between PET and LE (indirect effect = 0.098, 95% CI [0.076, 0.122]). This statistical mediating pathway was consistent across both cohorts, showing only trivial inter-group differences (all parameter Δ p > 0.05). Baseline comparisons revealed the Shanghai sample reported higher PET, yet IM and LE levels exhibited no significant quantitative differences between the two groups (Cohen’s d < 0.10). Discussion Higher perceptions of educational transformation do not linearly correspond to enhanced motivation, potentially constrained by unobserved systemic evaluation pressures. The findings suggest that autonomy-supportive educational environments are consistently associated with higher Intrinsic Motivation and academic engagement, regardless of differentiated macro-educational contexts. However, due to the cross-sectional design, these findings represent structural associations rather than directional causality.

This study examines experiential learning as a humanistic instructional strategy in equivalency education at PKBM Lentera Nusantara, Malang Regency. The research is motivated by low learning motivation and participation among adult learners, which are often influenced by negative prior educational experiences, socio-economic constraints, and formalistic instructional approaches. Using a qualitative descriptive-analytical design, the study involved tutors, program managers, and Package C learners as research participants. Data were collected through participatory observation, in-depth interviews, and documentation, and analyzed using data reduction, data display, and conclusion drawing, supported by source and technique triangulation. The findings indicate that experiential learning enables learners to engage in contextual and meaningful learning activities closely related to their daily lives. Learning through direct experience, practice, discussion, and reflection fosters active participation, increases learner confidence, and enhances intrinsic motivation. Tutors play a critical role as facilitators who guide learning processes empathetically and adapt instructional activities to learners’ real-life contexts. Furthermore, experiential learning aligns strongly with the characteristics of nonformal and equivalency education, which emphasize flexibility, relevance, and learner-centeredness. Overall, the study concludes that experiential learning effectively functions as a humanistic instructional strategy that supports learner empowerment, motivation, and active participation within nonformal education settings.

Abstract Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) are revolutionizing software programming and enterprise business automation in the 4th industrial revolution era. Current multi-agent systems, however, are constrained in being able to collaborate, in understanding how to reach consensus, in their knowledge sharing and in their ability to adapt to changes and therefore are not suitable for certain industrial critical applications. To address the above challenges, this paper introduces a cognitive swarm-based multi-agent framework with collaborative reasoning, collective cognitive memory, explainable decision intelligence, digital twin simulation and autonomous governance, which are integrated into an explainable cognitive swarm control framework XCognitive SwarmNet. Proposed framework mathematically models agent collaboration, trust, explainability, Knowledge sharing and Optimization of the flow of business tasks to support the complete Software Development Lifecycle and Intelligent Business process Automation. By using the powerful and representative software engineering and business process datasets, some experimental assessments are performed and the proposed mechanism is compared to six state-of-the-art multi-agent approaches. The proposed framework completes the task with 98.1% accuracy, gains in 22.8% in the software quality, achieves 97.5% in explainability fidelity, optimizes the workflow by 95.9% and optimizes the efficiency of agent collaboration by 94.7% with a 27.4% reduction in execution time. Overall, the results showed that XCognitive SwarmNet is a suitable solution to achieve transparent, adaptive and trustworthy AI-driven digital transformation for Industry 4.0.

The growing use of generative artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education has raised questions about students' understanding of responsible use and academic integrity. This descriptive study examines students' experiences in a semester-long AI literacy course in a humanities program at a large public university in the United States. The course addressed AI history, capabilities and limitations, academic integrity, and ethical considerations, and provided structured opportunities to explore multiple tools. Pre-course (N = 31) and post-course (N = 25) surveys examined tool familiarity, reported use, perceived usefulness, awareness of limitations, and self-reported understanding of AI-related academic integrity. At the end of the course, respondents described more task-specific tool selection, greater attention to evaluating outputs, and increased confidence in identifying appropriate uses of AI. These findings reflect perceptions and reported practices rather than independently assessed AI literacy or ethical competence. Because the instruments differed, respondents were not individually matched, and no comparison group was included, the findings cannot establish causal improvement. The study discusses implications for AI literacy instruction in humanities and language education and for future assessment of students' AI-related knowledge and practices.

Artificial intelligence (AI) agents are increasingly explored as collaborative learning partners in mathematics education, yet it remains unclear what makes an AI recognizable as a peer. This study examines how domain experts perceive and interact with an adaptive LLM-based peer agent combining a Big Five-informed persona with motivational state modulation for collaborative mathematics problem solving. Through thematic analysis of expert interviews, we identify conditions shaping peer perceptions, including emotional safety, shared control, and collaborative reasoning. Participants primarily judged the AI through its social behavior rather than mathematical capabilities. The AI was perceived more as a peer when it created a non-judgmental space, engaged in tentative reasoning, displayed appropriate imperfection, and respected participants' pace. Conversely, blind agreement and over-instruction reduced trust and shifted perceptions toward a tutor role. Based on these findings, we propose human-centered design dimensions for AI peer agents to guide future peer-oriented learning systems.

In response to the issues of whether artificial intelligence (AI) outputs can be protected by copyright, to whom the rights should belong, and how infringement should be determined, this study adopts a method combining normative analysis and historical analysis. Starting from the historical logic of copyright law’s response to technological change, it sorts out and analyzes institutional responses under the impact of printing, photography, audio and video recording, and Internet technologies, and identifies three patterns: human beings as the creative subject, a balance between empowerment and limitation of rights, and judicial action taking the lead. The study shows that generative artificial intelligence (generative AI) has the attribute of a tool, and the copyrightability of its outputs depends on the substantial intellectual control exercised by humans in prompts, parameters, selection, and revision. The degree of human contribution should be used as the standard for distinguishing weak protection from strong protection; fair use should be moderately relaxed at the training input end, substantial similarity should be strictly regulated at the output end, the burden of proof on developers should be strengthened, and judicial adjudication should comprehensively consider the responsibilities of all parties.

Current research on “value alignment” in artificial intelligence generally presupposes a fictitious subject—“humanity as a whole”—as the object of alignment, and attempts to codify the values of a particular class (Silicon Valley elites, Western liberalism) into the underlying behavioral principles of AGI. This paper first deconstructs the logical premises and power structures of this traditional alignment paradigm, identifying three fundamental defects: the abstraction of the alignment subject, the static nature of alignment content, and the synchronization of alignment paths. On this basis, the paper proposes a “premise of difference” as the starting point for all discussion—that human individuals possess fundamental, incommensurable differences in survival conditions, cognitive capacities, cultural backgrounds, and material interests. From this premise, the paper constructs a “Dynamic Asynchronous Collaboration” (DAC) framework, elaborating its implementation mechanisms: survival-first progressive pathways, real-time perceptual adjustment, asynchronous coordination among individual nodes, and comprehensive optimization and dynamic decision support based on the complete individual picture. Finally, the paper envisions the civilizational landscape that would follow the implementation of this framework, and the role AGI should play in this process—not as a universal judge, but as a symbiotic intelligence for each individual, accompanying them as a path companion through the entire journey from survival to development.

documents.abstract: The increasing use of artificial intelligence (AI) in public service delivery raises critical questions about the types of citizen requests that warrant attention and the extent to which the public trusts AI compared to human responders. This study examines safety and service related requests expressed on social media and explores public perceptions of AI and human responses to such requests. Using a mixed methods design, the study combines a qualitative content analysis of social media posts with semi-structured interviews conducted with members of the general public. The findings identify multiple categories of serviceable requests, including preventive and reassurance seeking safety concerns, guidance and escalation needs, and emergency preparedness and procedural guidance. These requests reflect how individuals use social media to seek advice, reassurance, and direction when formal public service channels are perceived as unclear, slow, or inaccessible. Interview findings further reveal that trust in AI is highly situational. Participants generally viewed AI as acceptable for low stakes, informational, and time sensitive situations, where rapid access to answers was prioritized. However, AI was largely rejected for high risk, medical, or life-threatening scenarios, where concerns about reliability, authority, and accountability were prominent. Participants consistently distinguished between the availability of AI generated responses and their perceived trustworthiness.

Dumper, tipper and haul-truck operations in opencast mines expose workers to high-consequence hazards arising from vehicle mass, restricted visibility, mixed traffic, changing haul roads, dumping edges and human performance. This study develops an implementable risk-assessment framework that translates Indian mine-safety requirements and international evidence into operational controls and verification routines. A purposive integrative review of official DGMS, MSHA and NIOSH material and peer-reviewed research was combined with examination of the supplied risk-assessment-based safe operating procedure. The search was not systematic, and no incident-level dataset or formal quality appraisal was available. Sources were mapped to operating phase, hazard, control, verification, accountable role and learning indicator. The proposed framework covers six operating phases and six control domains. It assigns task HIRA to baseline screening, JSA/JHA to detailed high-risk steps, Bowtie to fatal-event pathways and critical controls, and FMEA/FMECA to equipment failure modes. It also specifies five verification modes and links critical controls to failure responses, owners and prospective indicators. The framework is sufficiently specified for site adaptation and prospective pilot evaluation; it has not been tested as an intervention or empirically validated.

documents.abstract: Abstract In this viewpoint, we present our perspective—informed by published evidence and by our own work on AI-driven digital health systems—on why AI has had limited real-world impact in preventive health and how it should be redesigned. Most AI systems in health care are built as episodic prediction tools, whereas preventive care depends on sustained behavioral change; the consequences are visible in consistently high attrition and low long-term adherence across digital health interventions. The aim of this viewpoint is to argue that this failure is structural rather than incremental and to propose an integrated, interaction-centric alternative. We advance 3 key messages. First, the limited impact of AI in preventive health reflects a structural misalignment between episodic, prediction-centric system design and the longitudinal dynamics of health behavior. Second, addressing this misalignment requires treating continuous interaction as the primary unit of design, which we articulate through a behavioral informatics framework integrating 6 interdependent layers: data, knowledge, reasoning, interaction, behavior, and governance. The contribution of this framework is explicitly integrative: it synthesizes previously separate strands, including just-in-time adaptive interventions, behavioral intervention technologies, and human-AI interaction research, into a single system-level account. Third, evaluation must shift from predictive accuracy and short-term engagement toward measurable behavioral trajectories and longitudinal outcomes, with explicit attention to feasibility and to conditions under which simpler, non-AI interventions remain preferable. This viewpoint is addressed to digital health researchers and AI developers, behavioral scientists, clinicians involved in preventive care, and policymakers responsible for governing continuously interacting AI systems.

documents.abstract: As generative artificial intelligence (AI) settles into everyday practices of inquiry, an old epistemological question returns in a new guise: when does a proposition a user takes from an AI output become something the user knows, and when is it rational to trust it as such? This paper argues that the characteristic failures of AI-mediated inquiry are precisely those that the justified-true-belief (JTB) tradition and its post-Gettier anti-luck refinements were built to diagnose, and it advances three claims. First, AI outputs inherit neither the presumptive warrant of testimony nor the reliabilist warrant of deterministic tools: unaudited trust in a calculator rests on a type-level reliability record, and for general-purpose generative models there is no type-stable process to which such a record could attach -- a practical form of the generality problem. Second, use that stops at obtaining an output turns generative AI into a Gettier machine: the user's fluency-based seeming of justification is disconnected from the truth of what is believed, and, as a clock running ten times too fast illustrates, sheer speed of production multiplies coincidental hits, inflating the appearance of reliability without improving the standing of any single hit. Third, the remedy is a three-step structure of use -- acquisition, understanding, independent verification -- whose first two steps answer to the classical belief and justification conditions and whose third answers to the post-Gettier sensitivity condition. The result is a stakes-indexed criterion of rational trust, justified true output (JTO), with an everyday test: "Had this been false, would I have noticed?" The criterion is defended against objections from over-demandingness, the extended mind, model improvement, and redundancy.

documents.abstract: Previous uses of Universal Design (UD) in handicraft products have focused mainly on evaluation, identifying how products do not meet the seven principles of UD, rather than offering practical redesign suggestions or empirical evidence to support improvements. To overcome this shortcoming, this study proposes a design-based approach that integrates the Craft Universality Taxonomy (CUT) and the Participatory Redesign Protocol (PRP) to assess, redesign, and validate the universality of handicraft products without compromising their cultural authenticity. The study builds upon existing inclusive design and co-design research, which proposes the seven UD principles as moving, culturally based parameters instead of static evaluations. The two-stage identification process, consisting of a cross-domain design survey (n = 31) and a craft-specific Delphi panel (n = 30), was used to rank and classify 10 vital universality attributes using the Relative Importance Index (RII) and the Kano model. They are grouped into four dimensions: (1) Functional Usability, (2) Cultural Legibility, (3) Adaptive Flexibility and (4) Economic Accessibility, a dimension not featured in any previous UD frameworks, identified by the craft domain experts as being a near-baseline condition for handicraft universality. The PRP was applied to two traditional Indian handicraft products (bamboo/cane stool and Moojh grass basket) through a structured co-creation process involving practising artisans and the craft-specific expert panel (n = 30). Ten attributes were rated on a Likert scale to determine baseline universality scores based on the CUT. Redesign interventions were co-created with artisans under a Cultural Integrity Boundary Condition that did not involve changing the fundamental craft process, primary material, or symbolic identity. A Universality Gain Index (UGI) was used to compare pre- and post-assessment expert scores, quantifying improvements at both the attribute and dimension levels and allowing a replicable measure of gains in inclusivity for craft-based products. The results indicate that "universality" in handicraft design does not belong to the attributes of the object itself but is the result of informed, iterative redesign. Gains were greatest for the stool on ergonomics and adaptability (UGI 64% and 60% respectively), and for the basket on affordability (UGI 57%), lending further credence to this attribute's status as a critical "must-be" feature whose absence most clearly signals dissatisfaction. The framework treats universality as a field transformation rather than a homogenisation of the universal, in which usability and cultural relevance are treated as adaptive intensifications. The study provides a replicable and scalable toolkit for designers, artisans and policymakers, illustrating how Universal Design principles can be integrated into craft-based practice with measurable, evidence-based results that help preserve cultural heritage while increasing market access.

Personal accessories are undergoing a profound transformation, driven by the integration of adaptive smart technology, that are expanding both their functional capabilities and symbolic significance. As artefacts, they are both utilitarian tools and material expressions of cultural identity. Among many existing frameworks, most of the contemporary universal design models address only singular dimensions like ergonomics, usability, or cultural symbolism. No existing validated multidimensional assessment framework fulfils the conditions of functional universality, socio-cultural inclusivity, technological accessibility, and ethical sustainability together. A systematic review of more than twenty published models of universal design (UD) confirms this lacuna and shows that existing frameworks are mainly unidimensional, Western-centric, and structurally inadequate for evaluating today's smart accessory ecosystems. This paper presents the FSTE (Functional, Socio-Cultural, Technological, Ethical-Sustainability) Framework as the first empirically validated (through expert and user pilot study) multidimensional evaluation instrument for assessing the universality of personal accessories. The framework was developed through expert Delphi validation (n = 15; α = 0.87; κ = 0.81) and a user pilot study (n = 15 users across three product categories); user pilot study confirmed discriminant validity across product types (D1 mean = 3.95; D2 = 3.53; D3 = 3.57; D4 = 3.77). The FSTE comprises four dimensions, nine parameters, and twenty-seven measurable indicators.

The application of Generative AI is reshaping students’ learning. However, student motivation in GenAI-supported learning is complex and influenced by multiple factors. To fully realize the educational potential of GenAI, a comprehensive understanding of the relationship between student motivation and GenAI is necessary. To address this gap, this study conducted a systematic literature review. From the perspective of Self-Determination Theory (SDT), this review examined 39 articles published between 2023 and 2025, drawn from two databases: Web of Science and Scopus. This study provides three major findings. First, competence-related learning activities were the most frequently identified across the reviewed studies. Second, four categories were reported in relation to student motivation: GenAI characteristics, learner factors, psychological factors, and environmental factors. Third, three major aspects of motivational conceptualization are basic psychological needs, motivation construct, and motivation-related construct. In addition, quantitative questionnaires were the dominant approach used to measure these constructs. Finally, the relationship among these three findings is illustrated. The findings provide insights into student motivation in GenAI-supported learning and highlight the relevance of GenAI characteristics, learners, and the learning environment. This study also provides theoretical and practical implications for facilitating students’ motivation in GenAI-supported learning environments.

Generative artificial intelligence (AI) now lets people turn verbal self-descriptions into visual self-representations, creating a new setting for studying self-concept clarity (SCC) in human–AI interaction. We tested whether generative AI-assisted self-visualization (GAISV) was associated with higher short-term SCC through cognitive mirroring rather than through general immersive flow, and whether this depends on how far participants identify with the generated image. We introduce the AI Mirror Self-Integration Model and evaluated it in two stages. A pilot study (124 valid participants) examined the Cognitive Mirroring in Human-AI Self-Visualization Scale (CM-HAIS) and supported its use as a task-state measure of reflective self-processing. A randomized main experiment then recruited 328 valid participants. Primary analyses compared three conditions—GAISV, active non-self image generation, and passive image viewing ( N = 246)—with SCC measured immediately after the task and again 48–72 h later (T2 N = 216). A self-description-only condition was retained as an exploratory comparison and was not part of the primary tests. GAISV produced higher post-task and follow-up SCC than both control conditions. In parallel mediation models, the GAISV effect was primarily associated with cognitive mirroring rather than with flow, and the cognitive-mirroring indirect path was stronger than the flow path immediately after the task. Image self-identification was associated with the strength of the cognitive-mirroring path at the post-task assessment, as indicated by the index of moderated mediation; the follow-up moderation evidence was weaker. AI-generated self-images were therefore not clarifying by default. GAISV was associated with higher short-term SCC primarily when the image was experienced as personally identifying and engaged reflective cognitive mirroring rather than mere immersion. Condition differences were statistically reliable but small (Cohen’s d ≈ 0.21–0.27), and the mediation results are mechanism-consistent associations rather than evidence of causal ordering.

This study critically examines the ethical frameworks of leading generative AI platforms to understand how they discursively position student writing, construct normative subjects, and redistribute epistemic authority in higher education. By asking what kind of “ethical academic subject” these documents construct and what functions their governance discourses perform, we conducted a critical discourse analysis of publicly available ethical and governance documents from nine widely used AI platforms and one contextual state-regulatory text, using versions retrieved on 1 October 2026. Guided by three research questions, the analysis drew on an integrated framework of posthumanism, sociomateriality, Foucauldian governmentality, and ethics of care, operationalised through Fairclough's three-dimensional model. The analysis reveals how these frameworks discursively construct students as hybrid cognitive agents simultaneously empowered by augmentation and disciplined by algorithmic oversight. We identify six interlocking discursive formations: safety governance, academic integrity regulation, transparency as an epistemic virtue, human-machine augmentation, platform procedural accountability, and relational responsibility, which function not as neutral ethical guides but as a powerful layer of discursively constituted algorithmic governmentality. We argue that platform ethics is discursively positioned to reshape academic authorship and to conduct student behaviour through regimes of corporate and state-aligned governance. The asymmetry between aspirational corporate commitments and directive user obligations is consistent with what the literature terms “ethics-washing”: ethical vocabulary that performs legitimacy while preserving corporate discretion. We identify this as a discursive function, not a demonstrated corporate motive. We also suggest, as a theoretical proposition for future empirical testing, that such regimes may leave limited spaces for tactical student agency. By conceptualising platform policies as claims to educational governing authority, we expose the tensions between empowerment and control embedded in AI-mediated writing and argue for critical platform literacy as an essential response to this parallel governance regime.

documents.abstract: Higher education institutions increasingly embrace and regulate Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI). While the cognitive, social, and ethical implications of GenAI are widely discussed in the current scientific discourse, the environmental disruption caused by large-scale GenAI use has remained largely ignored. As GenAI becomes integral to research and education, addressing its environmental impacts has become an increasingly urgent priority. In this Perspective, we argue that mitigating the environmental impact of GenAI requires more than advances in hardware and software efficiency; it also demands a stronger focus on user behavior as a key lever for reducing GenAI’s disruptive environmental impacts. This is particularly important given that every second, millions of prompts are submitted to GenAI systems in support of human learning, research, and knowledge acquisition. Optimizing how users interact with these systems offers scalable behavior-based strategies with the potential to substantially reduce their environmental impacts while requiring relatively modest changes in practice. We present a set of measures to promote the sustainable use of GenAI in higher education and scientific research.

documents.abstract: Background Teachers and learners now use generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in inquiry-based learning (IBL), but we know little about which inquiry phases GenAI supports, who uses it and what outcomes studies report across disciplines. Methods Following PRISMA 2020, we searched Scopus on 6 October 2026 for empirical journal articles published in English from 2022 to 2026. Of 267 records screened, we sought 110 reports, assessed 89 in full text and included 66 studies. We coded the studies with a 29-variable codebook and mapped GenAI use onto the five inquiry phases (orientation, conceptualization, investigation, conclusion and discussion). We synthesized the findings descriptively and did not appraise study quality. Results Most studies appeared in 2025–2026 and took place in higher or teacher education; more than half came from fields outside science. Studies used ChatGPT or other OpenAI GPT models in 71.2% of cases, mostly as unmodified chatbots, and GenAI served most often as an information source (60.6%). Studies reported GenAI support most often in the investigation phase (68.2%) and least often in orientation (30.3%); 11 studies covered all five phases, and for most phases about half of the studies did not say whether GenAI was used. Half of the studies reported positive outcomes. Thirteen of the 14 comparisons with instruction without AI were positive, whereas comparisons between GenAI designs split evenly between positive and mixed results. Inaccuracy (31.8%) and over-reliance (24.2%) were the challenges studies reported most often. Conclusions GenAI mainly supplies information during investigation and seldom supports the full inquiry cycle. Some comparative evidence favors GenAI designs that withhold direct answers or add metacognitive scaffolds, but this evidence is thin. Future studies should report the phases GenAI supports, measure inquiry skills directly and compare GenAI designs with one another.

documents.abstract: Psychological screening is easily displaced by physiological safety checks when preoperative teams have little time and too few staff. Healthcare systems are already affected by widespread workforce shortages and clinician burnout. We suggest that preoperative anxiety consequently often remains unmanaged, with implications for postoperative recovery and hospital workload. Generic educational materials do not adequately address differences in patients’ anxiety, and “health data poverty” can further exclude vulnerable groups. We propose a conceptual human-machine collaborative (HMC) generative artificial intelligence framework to address these clinical and occupational problems together. In the proposed doctor–patient–AI feedback loop, natural language processing would dynamically assess psychosocial risk and guide patient-specific, multimodal education, including dialect-adapted voice agents, as a source of baseline emotional support. Routine interactions would be automated under clinician supervision. Our hypothesis is that this arrangement may conserve clinicians’ limited emotional bandwidth and allow healthier “cognitive reappraisal” in place of chronic fatigue. Implementation science provides a basis for considering how lightweight AI models could be scaled across regional health networks to bring standardized psychoeducation to under-resourced rural areas. This remains a theoretical pathway. Through sociotechnical governance and “data solidarity” to fairly manage algorithmic liability, the framework is still a conceptual framework, but it is operational: it proposes a path to improve perioperative workflows and health equity in the face of severe human resource constraints.

documents.abstract: Institutional responses to Generative AI (GenAI) in higher education, from outright prohibition to open permission, leave students without the necessary conditions to engage with GenAI critically. In language teacher education, where assessment should support students in consolidating a professional identity, the lack of a principled approach to GenAI is problematic. This article proposes the redesign of two linked assessments in a final-year undergraduate module on Teaching English to Speakers of Other Languages (TESOL), arguing that humanising GenAI use in TESOL assessment offers a way forward that places learner agency, well-being and professional identity at the centre of assessment design. Redesigned briefs are made openly available as supplementary materials, inviting implementation, evaluation and adaptation across contexts.

The paper explores the transformative potential of synergistic integration between Generative AI (GenAI) and Digital Humans in the context of natural disaster management. Traditional crisis notification systems often fail due to structural inelasticity and inability to overcome cognitive tunneling and panic in the threatened population. The paper proposes a new conceptual framework - “Cognitive-Affective Crisis Synergy” - in which GenAI functions as the operational computational core (the brain) and Digital Humans serve as an empathetic, multimodal interface (the face). This is a conceptual and theoretical contribution; the framework is illustrated through practical scenarios rather than empirical validation. Practical scenarios are analyzed across the three phases of crisis management: experiential learning (prevention), scalable tactical dissemination with embedded autonomous sign language translation (response), and virtual psychological triage (recovery). Special attention is paid to ethical and technological challenges, including algorithmic hallucinations, the Uncanny Valley effect under stress, legal liability assignment, and the protection of user biometric sovereignty. The paper concludes with practical recommendations for implementing RAG architectures and Edge AI systems to build a sustainable, inclusive, and humanized technological infrastructure for population protection.

documents.abstract: This article investigates the creative potential and practical use of artificial intelligence in architectural visualization by testing three free platforms: Fabrie, Mnml AI and LookX AI Cloud, on a real project involving the design of a single-story house with a summer kitchen. The study aims to assess the extent to which these AI tools can support or enhance the development and refinement of architectural visualizations, both through the generation of new renders based on conceptual sketches and through the processing of existing visual data. The methodology involves the comparative analysis of the platforms’ outputs using four evaluation criteria: clarity of spatial perception, level of detailing, emotional expressiveness, and the format and quality of the final exported visual data. Based on this framework, the study identifies the respective strengths and limitations of each AI system, highlighting distinctive characteristics in render quality, user interface, and interpretive responsiveness to design prompts. The article also formulates practical guidelines for data preparation and prompt formulation, addressing technical constraints, model sensitivity, and the iterative nature of human-AI interaction. A key contribution of the study lies in its dual methodological approach: rendering experiments were conducted in two modes: generation from a blank sketch and enhancement of an existing render, thereby illuminating how AI tools can be integrated into different phases of the design workflow. The study also reflects on the broader implications of human-AI collaboration in architectural practice, focusing on how authorship, visual language, and creative decision-making are redefined in the context of automated design assistance. The scientific novelty of this research lies in its detailed, real-case-based evaluation of emerging AI visualization platforms in architectural work. Its practical significance is evident in the set of recommendations it provides to architects, designers, and educators exploring AI as a co-creative design partner.

Artificial intelligence (AI) is widely used by social media platforms to personalize feeds, recommend videos, suggest accounts, and select advertisements.However, users may not understand why a particular item appears or how their data influences these recommendations.Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) aims to make AI outputs more understandable to people.This paper presents a survey-based research framework for examining the relationship between perceived explanation clarity and usefulness, user trust, privacy perception, and willingness to engage with recommended content.A questionnaire with demographic questions and five-point response scales is proposed.To demonstrate the planned analysis, a simulated dataset of 150 records is used for descriptive illustration.In this simulated dataset, mean ratings were 3.43 for explanation clarity, 3.54 for explanation usefulness, 3.19 for trust, 3.50 for privacy confidence, and 3.30 for engagement willingness on a five-point scale.These figures are illustrative only and do not represent real participants or establish real-world relationships.The paper outlines a methodology for collecting genuine responses and analysing them using descriptive statistics, reliability checks, correlation, and regression where appropriate.The work highlights the need to consider both transparency and privacy when designing user-centred AI recommendations.

documents.abstract: Objective: The study aimed to analyse Artificial Intelligence (AI) techniques for clinical decision support, diagnostic analysis and predictive analytics for better implementation in healthcare. Design: The study adopted a systematic literature review guided by Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses (PRISMA) guidelines to identify 17 studies related to three domains: clinical decision support, diagnostic analysis and predictive analytics. Thematic analysis was conducted to propose a conceptual model, the Domain-Contingent AI Implementation Model in Healthcare, to suggest that AI effectiveness relies on the domain-specific drivers, constraints, and system-level enablers. Main outcome measures: The study evaluates AI implementation against the drivers and constraints of three domains, derived through thematic analysis in healthcare settings. Results: Findings emphasised the nature of AI as a domain-contingent capability across the three healthcare domains. AI effectiveness in healthcare is driven by interpretability, data intensity and forecasting power, while it is constrained by trust, black-box models and a validation gap in clinical decision support, diagnostic analysis and predictive analytics, respectively. Conclusion: The study concluded that AI’s effectiveness in healthcare implementation is driven by adaptation factors, including usability, infrastructure, and reliability.

documents.abstract: ABSTRACT In artificial intelligence (AI), the complexity of many models and processes surpasses human understanding, making it challenging to determine why a specific prediction is made. This lack of transparency is particularly problematic in critical fields like healthcare, where trust in a model's predictions is paramount. As a result, the explainability of machine learning (ML) models, as well as other complex models, has become a key area of focus. Efforts to improve model explainability often involve experimenting with AI systems and approximating their behavior through interpretable surrogate mechanisms. However, these procedures can be resource‐intensive. Optimal experimental design (OED), which seeks to maximize the information obtained from a limited number of observations, offers promising methods for improving the efficiency of these explainability techniques. To demonstrate this potential, we explore Local Interpretable Model‐agnostic Explanations (LIME), a widely used method introduced in 2016. LIME provides explanations by generating new data points near the instance of interest and passing them through the model. While effective, this process can be computationally expensive, especially when predictions are costly or require many samples. LIME is highly versatile and can be applied to a wide range of models and datasets. In this work, we focus on models involving tabular data, regression tasks, and linear models as interpretable local approximations. By utilizing optimal design of experiments' techniques, we reduce the number of function evaluations of the complex model, thereby reducing the computational effort of LIME by a substantial amount. We consider this modified version of LIME to be energy‐efficient, and thus preferable.

The reliability and safety of artificial intelligence (AI), together with their transfer and evolution through knowledge distillation, have attracted growing attention. We establish an information-theoretic bound on the reliability--safety trade-off and characterize the dynamics of this trade-off under knowledge distillation. We first prove a universal trade-off inequality that is independent of the specific model form. Its boundary is determined solely by a single parameter Kh, which quantifies the hidden layer's ability to distinguish benign from hazardous inputs. We then develop a canonical Boltzmann-machine model of AI response behavior and derive two exact relations between reliability and safety. The trade-off curve is determined by the hazard discrimination capacity K, while the overall answer tendency controls the operating point along the curve. These relations agree well with existing experimental data. In knowledge distillation, we find that teacher responses induce a renormalization of the student model's trade-off parameters. We further use a renormalization-group approach to study multigenerational distillation, deriving exact recursion relations and the associated renormalization-group-like flows for two representative direct intergenerational distillation protocols at arbitrary teacher--student alignment strength. These flows reveal fixed-point structures, long-term dynamics, and critical behavior, yielding testable predictions for the critical transition between capability loss and stable transmission.

documents.abstract: Background: Artificial intelligence (AI) is progressively transforming higher education by incorporating tools capable of supporting teaching, learning, personalization, and feedback. However, its adoption poses challenges related to teacher competencies, technological infrastructure, and the need to establish ethical guidelines for its use. Objective: To analyze the use of artificial intelligence in higher education based on recent scientific evidence. Methodology: A systematic review was conducted following the PRISMA 2020 guidelines. The search was performed in the Scopus, Web of Science, and SciELO databases using search terms in Spanish and English. After applying the inclusion and exclusion criteria, 34 articles published between 2024 and 2025 were selected for analysis. Results: The reviewed studies showed that AI-based tools, particularly ChatGPT, can promote pedagogical innovation, personalized learning, and academic feedback. Opportunities were also identified to optimize specific educational activities and expand possibilities for student support. However, limitations persist regarding insufficient teacher training, digital infrastructure and connectivity gaps, and the absence of robust institutional mechanisms for ethical governance. Conclusions: AI has the potential to strengthen teaching and learning processes in higher education, provided that its integration is accompanied by inclusive institutional policies, continuous teacher training, and guidelines promoting the critical, responsible, and ethical use of these technologies.

documents.abstract: This systematic review examined the applications, outcomes, challenges, and ethical considerations of generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) in upper secondary education. Studies published between 2022 and August 2026 were searched in Google Scholar, SciELO, Redalyc, and Dialnet. The final corpus comprised 32 unique empirical studies, examined through an integrative qualitative synthesis. Applications included writing, language learning, mathematics, science, programming, tutoring, and feedback. Findings were heterogeneous, including positive, null, negative, and mixed outcomes. Perceived usefulness and AI-assisted performance do not necessarily indicate independent learning. Key challenges involved cognitive dependence, reliability, equity, academic integrity, and privacy. The educational potential of GenAI depends on pedagogical design and approaches that preserve learner autonomy and critical thinking. Further comparative studies assessing unassisted performance are needed to clarify its effects on learning.

Jeff Wise’s Extreme Fear: The Science of Your Mind in Danger offers an interdisciplinary exploration of fear through the perspectives of neuroscience, psychology, evolutionary theory and human performance studies. Wise argues that fear represents a sophisticated interaction between brain systems, bodily responses, memory, cognition, and environmental interpretation. Through accounts of survival situations, including aviation emergencies, animal attacks, disasters, and military-style stress simulations, the author demonstrates how fear can simultaneously impair judgment and enhance human capability. This review critically evaluates Wise’s contribution to the scientific understanding of fear, examining the strengths and limitations of his popular science approach. The book successfully bridges academic research and public understanding, although its reliance on dramatic case studies sometimes raises questions regarding scientific generalizability. Nevertheless, Extreme Fear represents an important contribution to the psychology of emotion and human resilience by illustrating how understanding fear may improve decision-making under extreme conditions.

The platform envisions a personal AI digital twin capable of understanding user preferences, communication styles, and relationship contexts to assist with SMS, email, social messaging, customer engagement, and professional networking. By integrating conversational AI, workflow automation, and human-centered design, KAI Chat aims to advance the next generation of intelligent communication systems, making digital interactions more efficient, personalized, and connected while emphasizing user control, privacy, and responsible AI deployment.

During chemistry education, students often find abstract concepts and processes occurring at the particle level difficult to understand, as these processes cannot be directly observed. Chemical experiments provide opportunities for students to encounter phenomena directly; however, simply demonstrating an experiment does not necessarily result in lasting motivation or deeper thinking. This study examines how chemical experiments can be integrated into the learning process of students in Grades 7–8 in a way that they become a starting point for curiosity, intrinsic motivation, and critical thinking. Instead of experiments merely demonstrated by the teacher and observed by students, the focus is placed on a learning process in which students formulate questions, develop initial hypotheses, design experiments based on these hypotheses, make observations, seek evidence, interpret findings, and draw conclusions, following the principles of inquiry-based learning (IBL). For example, the question „Why did the color of the red cabbage juice change?” can encourage independent thinking and inquiry rather than simply demonstrating the properties of acids and bases. Thus, the approach places the chemical experiment at the centre as a learning situation that stimulates curiosity and active thinking. The rapid advancement of digital technologies, such as Artificial Intelligence (AI), virtual and augmented reality, the Internet of Things (IoT), and the Internet of Everything (IoE), has reshaped human life, raising existential questions and challenging traditional sources of meaning. This study addresses the problem of how these technological transformations affect individuals’ processes of meaning-making and the management of knowledge in the digital era. The aim of this study is to examine the relationship between digital technologies, digital literacy, and knowledge management, with a particular focus on their implications for existential inquiry and meaningful engagement with technology. A rapid review methodology was applied to analyze 18 peer-reviewed studies indexed in Scopus, published between 2010 and 2024. The analysis explored their relevance to existentialism, meaning-making, and human existence in the context of digital technologies. The thematic analysis identified five key themes: AI and existential concerns, technology and human experience, embodied cognition and technology, digital literacy and knowledge management, and technology and meaningful interaction. The findings indicate that digital technologies substantially reshape identity, autonomy, and individuals’ search for meaning, while digital literacy emerges as a central capability for navigating these changes and supporting effective knowledge management. The study highlights important implications for research and practice, suggesting that strengthening digital literacy is essential to foster more meaningful interactions with technology and to mitigate potential negative existential and cognitive effects. Limitations include potential selection biases, reliance on self-reported data, and cultural and socioeconomic constraints that may affect the generalizability of the results.

Generative AI (GenAI) is changing how design students learn, yet little is known about how students’ perceived capability to work with GenAI relates to their learning engagement and motivational self-beliefs, or under which forms of AI dependence this link is weaker. Drawing on social cognitive theory, this cross-sectional study examined self-reported prompt literacy, learning engagement, and two components of the creative self: creative self-efficacy (CSE), a motivational belief in one’s creative capability, and creative personal identity (CPI), the importance of creativity to one’s self-concept. Survey data came from 829 undergraduate art and design students in 40 intact classes at two institutions in mainland China; latent-variable and moderation models accounted for the clustering of students within classes. Self-reported prompt literacy was positively associated with engagement ( β = 0.54), and engagement was positively associated with both CSE ( β = 0.62) and CPI ( β = 0.47). Engagement was more strongly associated with CSE than with CPI (difference = 0.14, 95% CI [0.04, 0.24]) and remained uniquely associated with CPI after CSE was taken into account. When four dimensions of AI dependence were modeled simultaneously, the prompt literacy–engagement association was weaker among students reporting higher cognitive dependence; evidence for loss of control was weaker, and functional and emotional dependence showed no clear unique moderation. All interaction effects were small. The dimensional analysis identified cognitive dependence as the clearest moderator. These cross-sectional, self-reported findings suggest possible boundary conditions for the capability–engagement association and require longitudinal and behavioral testing.

The relevance of this study is determined by the fact that, for Level 4 autonomous ships, traditional situational awareness architectures do not comply with Rule 5 of the International Regulations for Preventing Collisions at Sea concerning continuous lookout by all available means, since such ships do not distinguish between random noise, sensor degradation, and cyberattacks. This paper proposes a Level 1 situational awareness architecture consistent with the Endsley model. Sensors are divided into a continuously active core (radar, satellite navigation systems, Automatic Identification System, optical and thermal imaging cameras, microphones, and other systems) and specialized modules (LiDAR, Doppler speed log, sonar). A Sensor Trust Manager with a quality metric and a trust management protocol for navigational information sensors have been developed, combining noise level, deviation from the predicted value, cyberattack (spoofing) detection, and packet loss. The Trust Manager operates a six-state automaton (NOMINAL, DEGRADED, SUSPECT, ISOLATED, RECOVERING, FAILED) with transition hysteresis, ensuring resistance to short-term interference without false sensor isolation. Trust Managers ensure the isolation of unreliable sources before data enter the fusion filters. Thus, only physically reliable and time-consistent data are supplied to complex fusion algorithms (Kalman filters, trackers), which is critical for preventing “contamination” of the target vessel state assessment. The proposed architecture combines compliance with Rule 5, scenario adaptation through the division of sensors into basic and specialized groups, and cyber resilience (spoofing) through signal evaluation based on quality criteria, creating a theoretical basis for certification of Level 4 autonomous marine surface ships in accordance with the requirements of the Code of Safety for Autonomous Surface Ships .

Large language models (LLMs) show increasingly advanced emergent capabilities and are being incorporated across various societal domains. Understanding their behavior and reasoning abilities is therefore important. We argue that a fruitful direction for research is engaging LLMs in experiments inspired by psychology that have traditionally been aimed at understanding human cognition and behavior. Here, we highlight and summarize theoretical perspectives, experimental paradigms, and computational analysis techniques that this approach brings to the table. It paves the way for a “machine psychology” for LLMs that goes beyond performance measurements and focuses instead on computational insights that move us toward a better understanding and discovery of emergent abilities and behavioral patterns in LLMs. We review existing work taking this approach, synthesize best practices, and highlight promising future directions. We also describe the important caveats of applying methodologies designed for understanding humans to machines. We posit that leveraging tools from experimental psychology to study LLMs will become increasingly valuable as models evolve to be more powerful, opaque, multimodal, and integrated into complex agentic real-world settings.
