Digital transformation in the world of education requires teachers to be able to adapt to technological developments while developing learning that is creative, innovative, and in accordance with the needs of students. This community service activity aims to improve teachers' competence in utilizing digital technology as a medium and learning resource and encourage the creation of more interactive and student-centered learning. Activities are carried out through socialization, training, direct practice, discussion, and mentoring. Activity materials include the use of digital platforms and applications for learning, the development of interactive learning media, the wise use of artificial intelligence (AI), and strategies for designing digital-based creative learning activities. The results of the activity show an increase in teachers' understanding and skills in selecting, using, and developing digital technology to support the learning process. Teachers are also able to produce more interesting, interactive, and contextual media designs and learning activities. This activity shows that digital transformation is not only related to mastery of technology, but also to teachers' ability to integrate technology, pedagogy, and creativity to create meaningful learning experiences. Thus, strengthening teachers' digital competencies needs to be carried out in a sustainable manner so that teachers are able to become creative, adaptive, and innovative educators in facing educational changes in the digital era.

Generative artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping the cognitive conditions of knowledge innovation. While human–AI collaboration improves the efficiency of knowledge production, it may also induce creators to outsourcing cognitive work to AI systems. This study conceptualized this tendency as task-level metacognitive disengagement, defined as the immediate reduction of planning, monitoring, and reflection within a specific AI-assisted task, and, drawing on metacognition theory, cognitive offloading theory and self-regulated learning theory, examined its impact on knowledge innovation quality, its psychological mechanism, and boundary conditions through four complementary experiments. Experiment 1 showed that higher AI assistance significantly increased metacognitive disengagement. Experiment 2 revealed that cognitive offloading partially mediated the relationship between AI assistance and metacognitive disengagement. Experiment 3 confirmed the negative effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality, specifically on novelty, usefulness, and developability, with metacognitive disengagement partially mediating this effect. Experiment 4 tested the proposed moderated mediation model and found that task complexity strengthened, whereas individual AI literacy weakened, the negative indirect effect of cognitive offloading on knowledge innovation quality through metacognitive disengagement. These findings reveal a hidden cognitive cost behind the efficiency gains of human–AI collaboration and provide empirical evidence and theoretical implications for cultivating innovative talent and designing human–AI collaborative mechanisms in the era of artificial intelligence.

This study aimed to develop a causal relationship model and identify the direct and indirect effects of situational awareness on some basic futsal skills among fourth-year students at the College of Physical Education and Sports Sciences, Al-Qadisiyah University during the academic year 2025–2026. The research problem stemmed from observing student training sessions, revealing a significant disparity in cognitive abilities and skill-based decision-making despite their similar technical levels. The researcher employed a descriptive methodology using both survey and correlational approaches. The research population consisted of 100 students randomly selected and divided into construction pilot (20 students) and application (60 students) samples. A 14-item situational awareness scale was adapted for the sports context and its validity and reliability were verified (the corrected split-half reliability coefficient was 0.819 and Cronbach's Alpha was 0.866). The Statistical Package for the Social Sciences (SPSS) and AMOS software (v.24) were used to analyze the data. The results showed that students possessed a high level of situational awareness with a mean score of 33.090 and a standard deviation of 4.856. The study recommended incorporating the causal model into educational and training curricula to link cognitive-psychological factors with technical skill performance in futsal.

This chapter highlights the evolution of digital twins from passive data repositories to intelligent systems capable of contextual reasoning, supporting informed decision-making. We introduce the multi-aspect digital twin named MADT4BC, a core DYNABIC component designed to address the observability challenge and increase situational awareness in multi-scale critical infrastructures through AI-based assisting technology. MADT4BC reads and stores heterogeneous data streams from the physical infrastructure, connecting these to a semantically rich digital representation of real infrastructure using knowledge graphs. In response to user requests, AI agents are deployed to operate on top of the knowledge graph: creating, extracting, contextualizing, and reasoning over the collected operational data and the asset information to provide timely responses. We validate MADT4BC through one real-world use case, showcasing both knowledge creation and extraction abilities.

Authorship can align three relations to a work: experiencing it as one’s own, feeling like the agent behind it, and standing answerable for it. Effortful engagement can support this alignment, an arrangement this article calls the labor nexus of authorship, but direction, selection, editing, and authority over release also matter. Generative artificial intelligence can separate initial-production effort from the resulting product without uniformly weakening ownership, agency, or responsibility. This conceptual analysis specifies an authorship legitimation deficit as a mismatch between a particular authorship designation and the experiential or contribution-based grounds expected to support it under prior domain criteria. Separate ownership, agency, and community-warrant profiles distinguish an unsupported sole-creator claim from a supported editorial role, even when the person’s contribution and experience are unchanged. Historical precedents locate the problem within delegated and distributed making. The main contribution is a role-relative conceptual classification. Conditional relational hypotheses concern refusal or qualification of authorship (P4) and later recognition of alternative contributions (P6); agency and observer credit-blame hypotheses (P5a/P5b) concern constituent concepts rather than effects of the deficit. Market dependence suppresses observable disavowal when qualification threatens income; perceived system agency conditions felt answerability while assigned release duties remain fixed. Contribution records may assist later recognition but do not guarantee it. The framework identifies when a role exceeds its grounds while preserving supported AI-assisted authorship and accountability for release.

Giving empathy is good, but providing emotional support is hard work. Empathic AI gives cheap and easy support, but may be ethically costly. When AI provides empathy, people may feel less compelled to support others. Four studies provide evidence for “empathy offloading”: when people see AI as capable of empathy, they become less willing to empathize with the suffering of others, even without realizing it. When AI seems more capable of empathy, people—both with correlations (Study 1) and causal experiments (Study 2)—report more empathy offloading. When people learn that someone has received emotional support from large language models (LLMs), they engage less with others’ mental states (Study 3) and offer fewer empathic responses and more social judgment (Study 4). Empathic AI might provide emotional support at any time, but it may weaken our ethical and emotional commitments to fellow human beings. The implications of offloading emotional support may include empathic devaluing and atrophy, moral deskilling, and societal fraying.

University faculty members’ adoption of artificial intelligence (AI) technologies is important to the digital transformation of higher education, yet the motivational mechanisms associated with such behavior remain insufficiently understood. Drawing on self-determination theory (SDT), and the job demands–resources (JD–R) model, this study used a sample of 374 university faculty members to examine, through a moderated mediation model, the mechanism underlying the relationship between perceived craftsmanship spirit and AI technology adoption behavior. The results showed that perceived craftsmanship spirit significantly and positively predicted AI technology adoption behavior and that work engagement mediated this relationship. Challenge stressors negatively moderated the relationship between perceived craftsmanship spirit and work engagement and weakened the mediating effect of work engagement. These findings reveal the underlying pathway through which perceived craftsmanship spirit promotes AI technology adoption behavior and provide theoretical and practical implications for advancing the digital development and transformation of higher education.

BACKGROUND Virtual patients (VPs) are widely used in medical education, but creating high-quality cases requires clinical expertise, iterative revision, and alignment with educational objectives. Generative AI may support VP authoring, but direct comparisons between AI-generated and clinician-developed cases delivered within the same educational setting remain limited. OBJECTIVE This study aimed to compare medical students’ learner-perceived ratings of 1 AI-generated, expert-reviewed virtual cardiology patient scenario with those of 1 clinician-developed virtual cardiology patient scenario delivered through the same mobile platform. METHODS A randomized, participant-blinded 2-arm controlled study was conducted in October 2025 during scheduled fifth-year emergency medicine course sessions. Eligible participants were fifth-year medical students who had completed the cardiology course. Students were assigned 1:1 to complete either a clinician-developed VP (CD-VP; n=64) or a ChatGPT-generated VP (GPT-VP; n=67). Both scenarios followed a shared acute coronary syndrome blueprint and were delivered through the same mobile-optimized app (mobile VPs app [MobiViP]) with identical interface structure and branching logic. The GPT-VP was generated using GPT-5 and refined through iterative follow-up prompting under expert review; direct manual rewriting was prohibited. After completion, students completed a mandatory 19-item questionnaire covering realism and validity, cognitive load, self-reported learning and reflection, and engagement and satisfaction. Analyses included reliability testing, 1-sample tests against a neutral midpoint, Mann-Whitney U tests, and Spearman correlations. Full scenario content and development details are provided as multimedia appendices. RESULTS A total of 131 complete questionnaires were analyzed, with no item-level missing data. Mean subscale scores in the CD-VP group were 3.81 (SD 0.64) for realism and validity, 3.67 (SD 0.74) for cognitive load, 3.64 (SD 0.73) for self-reported learning and reflection, and 4.16 (SD 0.64) for engagement and satisfaction; corresponding GPT-VP scores were 4.11 (SD 0.56), 3.03 (SD 0.76), 3.86 (SD 0.77), and 4.28 (SD 0.58), respectively. Compared with the CD-VP, the GPT-VP received higher ratings for realism and validity (Mann-Whitney U=1503.0; P=.003) and lower cognitive load ratings, indicating a lower perceived burden (Mann-Whitney U=1070.5; P<.001). Self-reported learning and reflection showed a marginal difference between groups, with a higher rating for the GPT-VP (Mann-Whitney U=1719.0; P=.05), whereas engagement and satisfaction did not differ significantly (Mann-Whitney U=1922.5; P=.31). Internal consistency was acceptable to good for most subscales, although internal consistency for the realism and validity subscale in the GPT-VP group was moderate (Cronbach α=0.67). CONCLUSIONS In this single-center randomized study, 1 AI-generated, expert-reviewed cardiology VP scenario was rated similarly to or more favorably than 1 clinician-developed scenario in selected learner-perceived domains. Future research should expand to objective learning, retention, development workload, and scalability outcomes.

Background India's Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission (ABDM) is building a national digital health ecosystem. Uptake by health care providers remains uneven. Paper records often persist alongside digital tools, suggesting a gap between tool design and frontline care. Objectives To explore how health care providers and other stakeholders in two Indian states experience the usability of digital health tools under ABDM, how far they trust these tools, and what shapes their adoption in routine practice. Methods We analysed 42 in-depth interviews with state and district officials, frontline health workers, clinicians and implementation partners in Karnataka and Andhra Pradesh. Interviews were collected under the provider adoption objective of the parent Digital Health Exemplars: India study. We used template analysis, with Cognitive Load Theory and Human Factors Engineering as a priori lenses. The themes were then mapped to the Consolidated Framework for Implementation Research (CFIR). Results We identified six mismatches between tool design and clinical reality. These were (1) rigid interfaces that clash with nonlinear clinical reasoning, (2) separate portals that force repeated data entry, (3) fears of surveillance and unclear data use by AI tools, (4) reliance on paper and WhatsApp as practical workarounds, (5) unreliable networks, devices and power, and (6) one-time, generic training. In some settings, use appeared to depend on incentives and partner support. Conclusion Providers in this study did not avoid digital tools because of low digital literacy alone. They avoided tools that added work without clinical value. Sustained adoption under ABDM is likely to need interoperable, offline-capable tools, clear data-use safeguards and cadre-specific training, addressed in national implementation guidance alongside enrolment targets.

Introduction Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) can assist teachers with organizing information, generating alternatives, and drafting feedback. Its use in consequential judgments requires verifiable evidence and professional oversight. This study examines how teachers regulate optional GenAI assistance while preserving professional judgment. Methods Research on felt accountability, metacognitive monitoring, and AI literacy is conceptually integrated to develop a psychological process model of teacher decision episodes. Governance clarity is specified through rule clarity and role clarity, with responsible GenAI decision-making defined as regulated decision conduct. Results The conceptual analysis produces five testable propositions and one configurational expectation. Governance clarity is proposed to support responsible conduct through perceived accountability. Decision uncertainty is modeled as a metacognitive signal whose behavioral value depends on calibration and regulation; AI literacy is specified as a resource for verification, calibrated reliance, and appropriate escalation. Responsible conduct encompasses appropriate delegation, verification, calibrated reliance and accountable human authority, traceability, and escalation or override. These model outputs are theoretical propositions, not empirically established effects. Discussion The framework distinguishes generative assistance from conventional algorithmic advice and identifies task-dependent applications in assessment, feedback, referral, and student support. Future tests should compare unaided and assisted judgment, distinguish process quality from decision accuracy, and examine stakes, reversibility, and contextual dependence. Teachers retain authority to accept, modify, or reject GenAI output, or proceed without GenAI assistance.

The advancement of Generative AI (GenAI) technology has revolutionized the digital marketing sector, yet its impact on consumer psychology requires deeper understanding. Employing a Systematic Literature Review (SLR) approach based on the Scopus database, this study analyzes the relationships among GenAI usage, customer engagement, and customer trust. Literature mapping reveals that current research focuses on four primary clusters: consumer behavioral dynamics and purchase intentions, visual quality (hyperrealism), transparency and ethical issues, and collaborative creativity efficiency. Based on an analysis of these findings, the study identifies an "Authenticity Paradox," wherein AI-generated hyperrealistic visuals effectively boost purchase intentions but risk triggering the "uncanny valley" effect thereby undermining consumer trust if transparency is lacking. Trust is significantly shaped by the interplay between drivers, such as transparent labeling (watermarking), and inhibitors, such as visual artifacts and privacy concerns. Regarding engagement effectiveness, AI proves superior in stimulating interaction among existing followers, whereas human-generated content remains essential for reaching new audiences due to its empathy and emotional resonance. The study concludes that adopting a hybrid marketing strategy specifically Human-AI Co-Creation represents the optimal approach for synergizing GenAI's technological efficiency with the authenticity of the human touch in the long term.

Robotic Surgical Systems (RSS) have fundamentally transformed modern clinical therapeutics by enabling unprecedented precision, minimally invasive dexterity, and enhanced 3D visualization. However, the convergence of complex mechatronics, autonomous software algorithms, artificial intelligence (AI), and telesurgery presents unprecedented regulatory, ethical, and clinical risk profiles. This comprehensive review provides a rigorous comparative analysis of global approval pathways across four major jurisdictions: the United States (FDA), the European Union (EU MDR), Japan (PMDA), and India (CDSCO). We examine pre-market medical device classification, substantial equivalence standards, clinical evaluation requirements, cyber-security paradigms, post-market surveillance (PMS), and surgeon credentialing compliance. Furthermore, this paper critically addresses emerging regulatory hurdles surrounding generative AI integration, autonomous robotic navigation, liabilities in telesurgical latency, and data privacy frameworks. Recommendations are offered for establishing globally harmonized regulatory standards and adaptive oversight protocols to safe-guard patient safety while fostering technological innovation.

The rapid expansion of Generative Artificial Intelligence (GenAI) has unsettled established assumptions in language education. For University Language Centres (LCs) and Self-Access Language Centres (SALCs), AI systems offering instant feedback, writing support, language models, and conversational practice raise questions about their distinctive institutional roles. This opinion paper argues that LCs and SALCs should not compete with AI as providers of content or feedback. Instead, they should become human-centred mediating institutions that help learners, teachers, and institutions use AI critically, ethically, and pedagogically. After revisiting their established roles in supporting autonomous and self-directed language learning, the paper argues that AI demands a more cautious understanding of autonomy, as apparent independence may conceal overreliance, weak evaluative judgement, and outsourced cognition (Barrett & Pack, 2023; Fan et al., 2025; Zhai et al., 2024). It proposes five future functions of LCs and SALCs: AI literacy development, pedagogical curation, ethical mediation, reflective learner advising, and the integration of formal and informal learning. Drawing on the planned Language Education Institute at The Hong Kong Polytechnic University, the paper illustrates how language policy, technology-enhanced pedagogy, and human-centred education may be aligned. Ultimately, the value of LCs and SALCs lies in cultivating judgement, agency, accountability, and community.

Amid rapid generative AI growth, cultivating AI literacy among non-computer science (non-CS) undergraduates is a key higher education reform priority. Drawing on national policies and domestic course experience, this study constructs a five-dimensional progressive AI literacy framework: fundamental knowledge, risk identification, safety awareness, ethical analysis, governance participation. Pedagogically, the course uses an online smart platform for multimodal delivery, case-based teaching, and integrated process-team assessment. In a teaching practice of AI Safety, Ethics, and Governance with 66 non-CS undergraduates (44 valid surveys), results show a moderate positive correlation between classroom interaction and team project quality; students highly value innovative assessments like team projects and self-designed questions, and most gain achievement from work selected as teaching cases. This study offers an empirically grounded, data-driven course design and evaluation framework, filling the general education gap for non-CS students.

documents.abstract: Introduction Despite growing recognition that resilience and work engagement are central to employee wellbeing, the mechanisms through which resilience is associated with engaged work behaviour remain underexplored. Grounded in Conservation of Resources theory, this study examined task, cognitive, and relational job crafting as parallel mediating mechanisms in the resilience-work engagement relationship. Methods Cross-sectional data were collected from 332 employees at a large financial services organisation operating across South Africa and Namibia. Resilience, job crafting, and work engagement were assessed using validated measures. A parallel mediation model was tested using PROCESS macro Model 4 with 5,000 bootstrap samples. Results Resilience significantly predicted all three crafting behaviours and work engagement. All indirect effects were statistically significant. Cognitive crafting showed the largest estimated indirect effect, followed by relational and task crafting. The model explained 34% of variance in work engagement, with crafting behaviours accounting for approximately 45% of the total effect of resilience on engagement. The direct effect remained significant, indicating partial mediation. Discussion Resilient employees actively reshape their work through behavioural, cognitive, and relational crafting, and this proactive activity meaningfully explains how resilience generates engagement. Cognitive reframing of work as purposeful and meaningful emerged as the most potent pathway. Findings carry practical relevance for resilience training, leadership practice, and organisational job design.

documents.abstract: Background: As artificial intelligence (AI) systems move from supply chain decision support towards operational execution, governance must distinguish technical capability from permissible decision authority. This study develops a reversibility-aware framework for allocating human–AI control according to decision risk, recoverability, uncertainty and consequence propagation.Methods: A design science research-inspired approach was used to operationalise four constructs on normalised scales and integrate them into an equally weighted Decision Control Score (DCS), supplemented by governance overrides. Five control modes, from HC-0 (human-controlled) to HC-4 (monitored AI execution), were evaluated using six author-constructed supply chain scenarios. The framework was compared with illustrative fixed HC-3 and risk-only baselines, followed by reversibility and weighting sensitivity analyses.Results: The framework assigned HC-4 to routine inventory replenishment, HC-3 to forecast adjustment and purchase-order quantity modification, HC-2 to logistics rerouting, HC-1 to supplier selection or replacement, and HC-0 to critical supply interruption response. Its recommendations differed from the risk-only baseline in two of six scenarios. When the other constructs were held constant, varying reversibility changed the logistics-rerouting control mode. Across four alternative weighting configurations and six scenarios, 23 of 24 classifications matched the equal-weight results (95.8%).Conclusion: The analytical evaluation illustrates how recovery feasibility can affect rule-based control allocation. Because scenario inputs, weights, thresholds and safeguards were stipulated rather than empirically calibrated, these findings do not establish operational effectiveness or predictive validity. Independent expert assessment and field validation are required before implementation.

documents.abstract: This paper examines the limitations of artificial intelligence–driven managerial rationality in top management, with a focus on agent-based AI models. This study employs a systematic literature review using a PRISMA-inspired approach to analyze agent-based AI models in executive decision-making contexts. Drawing on the contemporary scientific literature, the study conceptualizes AI as a probabilistic decision-support mechanism rather than an autonomous managerial actor. The paper identifies key structural and epistemic constraints of agent-based AI, including probabilistic outputs, bounded rationality, and contextual dependence, emphasizing the need for sustained human participation and oversight in executive decision-making.

documents.abstract: The increasing integration of GenAI into academic writing has prompted renewed attention to how students engage with writing tasks in English for Academic Purposes (EAP) contexts. While existing research has focused on the capabilities and risks of GenAI, less attention has been given to the instructional conditions that shape how students use these tools. This paper proposes the Rigor–Commitment Alignment Framework (RCAF), a conceptual model that examines the interaction between academic rigor and teacher commitment as two dimensions of the pedagogical environment. Drawing on research in academic literacies, engagement theory, self-determination theory, and visible learning, the framework identifies four instructional configurations (Neglectful, Indulgent, Punitive, and Rigor with Support) and links them to four engagement profiles (deep-agentic, surface, strategic, and disengaged). The framework is further grounded in a triadic reciprocal model in which instructional conditions and student engagement are dynamically interrelated. The analysis suggests that patterns of GenAI use are not primarily determined by the technology itself, but by the interaction between task demands, instructional support, and student engagement. In this context, GenAI may either support higher-order academic literacy practices or facilitate low-effort task completion, depending on the alignment between rigor and commitment. The RCAF provides a conceptual basis for examining these dynamics and offers implications for EAP pedagogy and AI policy.

Ensuring business continuity in critical cyber–physical infrastructures requires a holistic risk management approach that anticipates, quantifies, and controls complex cascading effects across interdependent services. This chapter presents the solution approach developed by the DYNABIC project, which pivots around RISKM4BC , a reusable methodology and supporting tools to manage risks that affect business continuity. The approach integrates: (i) a Bow-tie Smart Center that structures threats, barriers, and consequences and is augmented with information from Large Language Models (LLMs) to enrich scenario coverage and generate mitigation recommendations; (ii) predictive business process monitoring that forecasts the performance and risk of incident response workflows; and (iii) a cascading risk model that, based on Bayesian networks, quantifies interdependent risk exposure and updates it in near real time when new evidence arrives. The methodology is operationalized through traceable risk profiles and goal-oriented aggregation that align model outputs with business objectives, as well as through user-facing views that connect live evidence to decisions. A high-level architecture describes how these components interact with monitoring and digital-twin data to maintain a live risk picture for decision making of both human operators and automated responses. A running example from transportation infrastructure (by Ferrovial) illustrates how the methodology produces actionable risk alerts (e.g., congestion likelihood and business impact level), anticipates resolution timelines, and evaluates exposure to external dependencies (e.g., power or communications). We conclude the description of the approach with methodological advantages, lessons learned, and future extensions, including business-goal linking, automated incident reporting, and interactive what-if analysis.

The acquisition of English as a second language (L2) is increasingly shaped by rapidly changing educational, social, technological, and digital environments, particularly in the age of Artificial Intelligence (AI). This study investigates the acquisition of English as a second language from the perspectives of students, teachers, and parents, with particular attention to the dynamic interaction of individual, familial, classroom, and technological factors. Guided by Complex Dynamic Systems Theory (CDST), the study conceptualizes English language acquisition as a dynamic and interconnected process that develops through the continuous interaction of multiple contextual and individual variables. A case-study research design was employed, and purposive sampling was used to select participants from Punjab, Pakistan. The study comparatively examines patterns of convergence and divergence across these three stakeholder perspectives to develop a multidimensional understanding of English L2 acquisition in the contemporary AI-mediated learning environment. Its practical implications extend to students, parents, teachers, educational institutions, policymakers, curriculum developers, and teacher-education programmes by informing the development of more responsive and technology-integrated approaches to English language learning. Furthermore, the findings may provide insights for AI and NLP developers, digital learning designers, social-media platforms, and digital content creators to develop linguistically accessible, learner-centred, and context-sensitive English-learning resources. Overall, the study seeks to contribute to a more comprehensive understanding of how multiple stakeholders perceive and experience English L2 acquisition in an increasingly AI-driven educational landscape.

Critical Infrastructures (CIs) are increasingly complex cyber-physical systems whose interdependencies expose societies to cascading failures triggered by cyber and physical threats. Traditional risk assessment methods and intrusion detection systems are insufficient to address rare, high-impact, and unforeseen attacks, highlighting the need for resilience-oriented approaches that extend beyond prevention. This chapter presents AWARE4BC, a framework developed within the DYNABIC initiative to enhance CI resilience and business continuity through Digital Twin–enabled services. AWARE4BC integrates continuous infrastructure monitoring, advanced attack and anomaly detection, and holistic resilience assessment based on runtime observations. It leverages heterogeneous data sources, uncertainty-aware reasoning, and semantically enriched threat indicators to support real-time situational awareness and evidence-based decision-making. Resilience is quantified through effectiveness and resilience curves capturing degradation, absorption, recovery, and adaptation across multiple concerns, including technical, economic, environmental, and social dimensions. The framework’s practicality is validated through a hackathon-based evaluation using a transportation use case, demonstrating its ability to detect both known and zero-day attacks and assess their cascading impacts. Results confirm the added value of combining security monitoring with resilience assessment. AWARE4BC offers a generic, modular approach applicable across CI domains, contributing to more robust and adaptive protection of essential services.

documents.abstract: This systematic review and meta -analysis estimated the prevalence of sharps injuries among healthcare waste workers (HWW) and evaluated hepatitis B virus (HBV) vaccination coverage and HBV and hepatitis C virus (HCV) infections. PubMed, Scopus, Embase, LILACS, SciELO, the Virtual Health Library, the CAPES Periodicals Portal, and Google Scholar were searched through 19 May 2026. Twenty-two studies involving approximately 9,000 HWW and 1,722 sharps injuries were included. Random-effects meta -analyses used logit transformation and restricted maximum likelihood estimation. The pooled prevalence of sharps injuries was 34.1% (95% CI, 22.8–47.5%), with substantial heterogeneity (I 2 = 98.9%). HBV vaccination coverage was 31.1% (95% CI, 8.2–68.3%) and was not associated with sharps injury prevalence (β = 0.338; p = 0.544). Pooled HBV and HCV prevalence estimates were 2.3% (95% CI, 0.3–15.4%) and 3.36% (95% CI, 1.17–9.23%), respectively. No HCV seroconversion was reported in follow-up studies. Approximately one-third of HWW experienced sharps injuries, highlighting the need to strengthen waste segregation, personal protective equipment use, biosafety training, HBV vaccination, and occupational surveillance to improve worker safety and reduce preventable blood-borne infections.

With the rapid uptake of artificial intelligence (AI) in higher education, academic risks need to be viewed as not only technical issues but as socio-institutional harms that impact equity, trust, and accountability. The methodology used for this study is a conceptual literature review and qualitative synthesis of existing academic research. This study tackles the problem existing in the literature, which is unstructured definitions, by synthesizing the literature to create a complete conceptual framework for Social Risk Management (SRM). The proposed framework places SRM in a unique role, serving as the institutional interface between the introduction of AI and social outcomes, with the role of a mediator and moderator between the raw technical inputs and the negative effects of AI on society. There are four main operational pillars of SRM identified in the synthesis. This study also adds the competency of SRM as a core competency of governance, not only for its ethical dimension but also for being a proactive competency. Moreover, it offers a clear research program for future empirical studies, detailing potential ways to measure SRM and to investigate its differences in various application areas of universities, such as admissions, financial aid, tutoring, and even assessment.

Abstract AI systems increasingly serve as social partners, companions, and romantic partners, yet governance remains fragmented, reactive, and split between clinical applications and anthropomorphic deception. Current Canadian AI regulation (PIPEDA and the un-proclaimed AIDA) addresses privacy and market access only, while Character.AI and a growing list of anthropomorphic-chatbot suicide cases point directly to the product-liability question that no Canadian instrument answers. This gap illustrates the regulatory break that motivates this paper. In the physcial world, the ethics → policy → engineering loop (EPE loop) works as a mutually protective cycle in which ethics specifies the values a system must serve, engineering builds mechanisms that support them, and policy verifies and enforces them, so that companies and stakeholders share benefits from a standardized technique world. Virtual AI services and products, however, do not inherit that protection. Their values are relational, their mechanisms conversational, and their harms uncodified, so the EPE loop does not close. This systematic review of 169 studies examines where the loop breaks. This systematic review examines how engineering, ethics, and policy shape human-AI relationships between 2022-2026 and identifies challenges and opportunities at their intersections. Following PRISMA 2020, seven databases yielded 395 records; 169 studies met inclusion criteria. Reflexive Thematic Analysis and K-means clustering synthesized our findings. We identify three distinct clusters. The empirical group (n = 30) is characterized by empirical research that documents deception and vulnerability but lacks governance support, producing a regulatory gap. The anthropomorphism group (n = 83) focuses on engagement and safety, and is characterized by the highest standardization gaps that is mostly implicit stated, meaning researchers name the harms but never specify the technique standards against which those harms would be measured. The clinical group (n = 56) shows strong policy engagement but the largest conceptual framing gap, and its high principle-to-practice gap indicates that the gap becomes visible precisely because its principles are codified, yet the cluster lacks broad conceptual exploration of additional missing values such as relational and communicative harms. We show that the three governance failures are three skipped Value-Senstive-Design (VSD) obligations: technical (Cluster 1), conceptual (Cluster 2), and empirical-to-instrument (Cluster 0). We propose a research agenda that closes each gap. For anthropomorphic AI, technique solutions developed into technical standards; for highly regulated domains, broader conceptual maps of the values they have not yet admitted; and, across all three clusters, stakeholder-anchored empirical work under VSD framework. We further argue that VSD values are not exhausted by design values but include ethical values and, potentially, policy values, which is what allows the EPE loop to rotate again. So that the next anthropomorphic-AI suicide case could be decided by a standard rather than by a motion to dismiss.

documents.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) are increasingly used for learning, raising a key question: can learners remain epistemically proactive, retaining responsibility for the cognitive and regulatory activities through which learning is produced while working with AI? Because this responsibility may change as interactions unfold, we examine epistemic proactivity as a developing process. We conceptualize epistemic proactivity through self-regulated learning (SRL) moves, complemented by help-seeking strategies and manifestations of epistemic vigilance. We analyzed these behaviors in 880 substantive turns from 112 secondary-school students completing open-ended mathematical-modeling practice with a general-purpose LLM (Mistral). Overall, students showed limited observable epistemic proactivity: their interactions were strongly request-dominated, with planning, monitoring, and evaluation relatively rare, although low-quality AI responses elicited more explicit evaluation. Temporal analyses qualified this picture: explicit SRL-related moves increased modestly over the chat, but help-seeking strategies became less understanding-oriented. Crucially, these temporal trajectories in help-seeking strategies predicted their post-test performance without AI beyond pre-test and aggregate patterns: students whose requests became more understanding-oriented performed better once AI assistance was removed. Thus, while students had a limited epistemic proactivity overall, its temporal development still was a critical predictor of post-test performance without AI. These results underscore the importance of examining the temporal organization of epistemic proactivity, rather than isolated prompt types, for understanding AI-supported learning. We release our fully-anonymized dataset publicly in an OSF repository.

Topics include the emergence of computational ophthalmology, the role of big data in scientific discovery, the application of machine learning to ophthalmic imaging, and the development of artificial intelligence (AI)-ready data ecosystems. documents.abstract: The integration of Computational Thinking (CT) into mathematics education frequently encounters challenges within Digital Mathematics Learning Environments (DMLEs), which often adopt static, one-size-fits-all approaches that fail to adequately support learner diversity. While prior studies have identified distinct learner personas—such as the Frustrated Perfectionist and the Conceptually Stalled Learner—a critical barrier remains in scaling personalized, real-time pedagogical support. This study proposes a novel framework utilizing Generative AI (GenAI) to transform DMLEs into dynamic “co-thinkers.” Employing a two-phase design-based research methodology, we first empirically validated a four-persona typology through qualitative analysis and quantitative behavioral signatures. Subsequently, we developed and expert-validated a conceptual GenAI scaffolding prototype, comprising structured prompt templates engineered to deliver metacognitive and affective support tailored to individual persona needs. Preliminary expert validation confirms pedagogical soundness and highlights key ethical considerations. The paper presents this integrative framework alongside a detailed discussion of its design principles, operative AI cycle, and embedded ethical safeguards, positioning persona-aware AI as a transformative, yet responsible, pathway for computational mathematics education.

documents.abstract: This chapter introduces the DYNABIC framework, a comprehensive and adaptive cybersecurity solution designed to enhance the resilience of Critical Infrastructures (CIs) in the face of evolving cyber-physical threats. The framework integrates advanced technologies such as digital twins, artificial intelligence, and cyber threat intelligence to enable real-time threat detection, simulation, and response. At its core, DYNABIC employs a bidirectionally synchronized digital twin to model and simulate cyber-physical systems, supporting dynamic risk mitigation and adaptive response strategies across the four phases of the resilience cycle: Plan/Prepare, Absorb, Recover, and Adapt. The architecture is modular and scalable, fostering collaboration among CIs and Computer Security Incident Response Teams (CSIRTs). It includes key components such as MADT4BC, SOAR4BC, RISKM4BC, SIM4BC, AWARE4BC, and CTI4BC, which collectively support real-time monitoring, risk assessment, incident simulation, automated response, and threat intelligence sharing. The framework also incorporates a human-in-the-loop interface (AVATAR4BC) to enhance situational awareness and decision-making.

This study examines the effect of transformational leadership and employee engagement on employee performance within the service industry. As organizations in this sector increasingly compete on service quality, customer satisfaction, and operational efficiency, understanding the human factors that drive employee performance has become a strategic priority for management. Transformational leadership, characterized by idealized influence, inspirational motivation, intellectual stimulation, and individualized consideration, is theorized to enhance employees' motivation, commitment, and willingness to exceed expected job requirements. Similarly, employee engagement, reflecting the degree of vigor, dedication, and absorption employees exhibit toward their work, is considered a critical psychological state that translates leadership influence into tangible performance outcomes. This research employs a quantitative approach using a survey method distributed to employees working in service-based organizations. Data were collected through structured questionnaires measuring transformational leadership, employee engagement, and employee performance, and were analyzed using multiple regression analysis to test the proposed hypotheses. The findings reveal that both transformational leadership and employee engagement have a positive and significant effect on employee performance, whether tested partially or simultaneously. Transformational leadership was found to strengthen employees' sense of purpose and trust in their leaders, which in turn fosters higher engagement and, consequently, improved performance outcomes. Employee engagement was also identified as a key mediating mechanism linking leadership behavior to performance results. These findings contribute to the growing body of literature on leadership and human resource management by providing empirical evidence from the service industry context, where interpersonal interaction and employee behavior directly affect service delivery quality.
